prompt: A square has four sides and a foot has five

units.explanation: Broad early head, measured on every token including the first. Predict plain English prose active-weak about one text in four, at 0.25-0.37 of max. Those peaks fall on the first to fourth token, for example on first tokens such as 'She', 'We', 'Our', 'My', 'Many', 'After', 'So', 'Yes' or 'Let', which alone reach 1.1-1.8. Predict non-English Latin-script prose (Turkish, Polish, Portuguese, German, Spanish) active on nearly every token. It is strongest (0.5-0.75 of max) on and after diacritic or byte-fragment tokens such as ' ç', 'ż', ' iç', 'ö' or 'ð', even when only one such word sits in an English sentence. The head is also strong (0.4-1.0) on the newline that ends a code or block-comment line when earlier lines began with the same indentation or ' *' token (it attends back to those tokens), and on chained ' -'/' +' operators in 'Let d(j) = 0 - j - 2*j - 9 + ...' arithmetic. The only class predicted inactive is a numbered English list item: a whole text made of one digit 1-9, a period, a space and one plain all-English sentence, 7-15 tokens in total (e.g. '4. The bridge was closed for repairs last summer.'). 27/27 such texts measured below the line, with a highest peak of 0.86 (0.19 of max). Short texts that lack this prefix (one-word sentences, word lists, integer lists) are NOT predicted inactive, and the prefix does not quiet non-English sentences.

Duplicate-token head whose attention on a word's first occurrence is drained by every earlier 'sink' token in the text (commas, periods, line breaks, '(' and the words the/a/an/in/for/to/on/of/and): a word or name fires on first occurrence only when at most one sink precedes it after the text's first token ('Gerda Gilboe', 'Then we saw Sandusky', 'My uncle told me that he met Hartley'; names stay active after one sink, at about 0.25-0.5 of max), and once three or more sinks precede it only a token with an earlier copy in the text fires: the second or later copy of a capitalised name or rare word/code piece (' Hart' in 'roads to Hartlepool ... letters from Hartlepool', ' Prec', 'Value' in 'getValue ... setValue'), strongest on long-range repeats and third copies. Predict inactive any text whose first content word (after its first token) comes after at least two sinks ('Then, in the ...', 'It was in the ...', 'So, in the ...') and in which no capitalised name or rare piece occurs twice; first-occurrence names, numbers, punctuation runs and function words there stay inactive (the one known exception is ' Ger' of Gerlach), while a common lowercase word repeated in such a text, or a content word after exactly one sink ('In the office nobody wanted'), is unreliable and not claimed either way.

Broad early-position head: predict almost any text active-weak (about 0.25-0.5 of max), because its first ~7 tokens after the opening one (ordinary prose, code, HTML, a short sentence) cross the line, while tokens deeper than ~10 positions are weak. It is strong (about 0.45-1.0 of max) on the line break(s) that end a short opening line of 1-5 tokens, such as a title, name or header ('Carl Nielsen

', 'package config

', 'x = 1
'). Texts that are only a comma-separated list of plain numbers ('3, 7, 12, 45') stay inactive (below 0.2 of max), as does replacing the title's line break with a comma, period or semicolon (which drops it back to the weak band).

L2/H1 is a pure previous-token head: 0.91 of its attention is on t-1 on random repeated sequences (duplicate 0.00, induction 0.00) and 0.68-0.97 at word positions of ordinary text (a sentence-final '.' gets 0.01), so its strength |W_O(z - mean z)| at a position measures how far the token BEFORE the peak stands from the head's average write, not the token it sits on: in 'The map shows Yuri in the corner.' ' Y' scores 0.00 and the next piece 'uri' 1.10, while the whole-word version 'the man' scores 0.02, and after the same piece ' methyl' the following token barely matters ('gly' 1.95, ' group' 2.22, ' here' 2.14, ' in' 2.25). Predict active (1.0-3.7, well above the 0.94 line = 0.25 x the scan's 3.747 max) when the token before the peak is a piece rather than a whole word - any non-Latin byte piece (26 of 28 tested sentences across Greek, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Bengali, Thai, Arabic/Urdu, Hebrew, Hangul, Han, German, Finnish, Turkish, Vietnamese and Afrikaans scored 1.0-2.2), a word-internal piece of a split Latin-script word or name ('ph' 1.6-3.0, 'oo' 2.06, 'ak' 1.85, 'ost' 1.85, 'ip' 1.78, 'Br' 1.72, 'Sh' 1.98, ' methyl' 1.95-2.25), or a piece of an all-caps or hex identifier ('IN' 1.45, 'JA' 1.71, hex 'bf' 2.19) - predict inactive (0.00-0.6) when every token before a candidate peak is a whole high-frequency English word, punctuation or a newline (' the', ' of', ' and', ' house', ' people', ' city', ' water' 0.00-0.19; ten all-common-word sentences 0.00-0.18; comma-separated lists of single common words 0.00-0.58; '100 200 300 400 500 600 700' 0.00), and predict only weak, at or just over the line (0.4-1.3), after an ordinary whole English content word, which crosses in about one plain sentence in six (' short and' 1.29, ' light and' 0.99, ' first item' 1.00, 'Best wishes' 1.08, ' May and' 0.93) and stays below in the rest (' warm and' 0.15, ' old man' 0.65, ' sat down' 0.64, ' run in' 0.53, ' long decline' 0.37).

L2/H7 is a retrospective local head: it attends over the previous one to four tokens (chiefly two back, with previous-token score 0.26 and duplicate/induction scores 0.00) and its write to the residual departs from its mean output only where that window is filled with word-internal subword fragments rather than space-initial whole words. On 273k tokens of the scan corpus 19% of word-internal fragment positions are active against 4% of space-initial ones (Indic 50%, Hebrew 46%, Thai 44%, Arabic 39%, Greek 37%, Cyrillic 30% of fragment positions), and activity climbs monotonically with the length of a fragment run (2 hex chunks 0.70, 3 chunks 1.15, 4 chunks 1.38, 6 chunks 2.04 of max), so it fires inside long numbers, hashes, DOIs, versions, IPs and identifier pieces and in densely fused non-Latin script, while ordinary English prose, a single number, date or rare word inside a sentence, whole-word English tokens and sequences of unrelated tokens stay inactive.

Active (above 0.25 of max) on (1) every '\n' token that has another newline token among the previous 4 tokens (blank lines, short lines such as headings, 'A:', menu items; peak 0.5-0.9 of max), or that ends a line whose last token is '.', '?', ':', '{' or ').' (0.27-0.4), while a lone '\n' after a word, number, comma, quote or closing bracket stays inactive; and (2) in running prose, only on the word right after ' is', ' was', ' are', ' has', ' in', ' at' or sentence-initial 'In' when that word is a determiner, possessive or quantifier (the, a, an, my, her, this, one, what, all) or 'In addition/fact/order/terms' (0.26-0.44), plus, about 40% of the time, the curly apostrophe after a pronoun in contractions like 'I’m'. Every other prose token, including determiners after ' to', ' on', ' with', ' by', ' from', ' and', ' that', a comma or a noun, is predicted inactive; ' of the' and ' for the' are borderline (about 0.22-0.25, mostly inactive).

Broad previous-token head: predict ordinary prose active-weak (most sentences cross the line somewhere), with activity on the words that open the object of a verb or preposition (the 'the'/'a'/'their'/'me'/name right after 'told', 'reminded', 'gave', 'on', 'in', 'of', 'to', 'from'), attending to that governing word and fading over the noun phrase, and strongest (up to max) on such a determiner after a speech verb deep in a long passage (', told the Providence Journal'). Predict whole texts inactive only when they are entirely one of these: a bare noun phrase with no preposition ('The tall building.', 'My brother and his friends.'); interjections, discourse words and punctuation ('Yes. No. Maybe.', 'Well, then, and so.'); a two- or three-word intransitive clause ('She smiled.', 'The bell rang.'); or a copular clause 'The N is/was ADJ.' — any verb or preposition followed by its object (e.g. 'Then he told them,') makes a text active.

Broad, mostly previous-token head: predict ordinary prose active-weak (most sentences of a dozen or more tokens have one or two tokens just over the line, roughly 10% of tokens, peaks near 0.3-0.45 of max), and it is strong (above ~0.6 of max) on a content word, or a later sub-word piece of a name or term, whose attention falls almost wholly (weight ~0.9) on the specifier opening its phrase: 'which' ('regardless of which system'), numerals ('the two Kivu'), 'every', 'any', possessives 'its'/'their', 'a' after a preposition ('At a global'), 'of' in 'some of / one of' before a name, 'are' in 'There are further', or the head noun before a name ('regional capital Białystok'); it is weak after 'the', 'this', 'that'. Comma lists of plain numbers and strings of one-word exclamations ('Stop. Yes! Okay?') are inactive.

Broad previous-token head: predict ordinary prose, code and number lists active-weak (about 0.25-0.55 of max), but predict inactive a two-token text made of one lowercase common word that is a single token followed only by '.', '!' or '?' (e.g. 'cat.', 'road!', 'tree?'; capitalised words like 'Okay.' and words split into pieces like 'gar|den.' do not count). It is strong (above about 0.6 of max) on the second piece of a word split into sub-word tokens after a short, usually capitalised or all-caps, word-start fragment it attends to (GRE|ATER, PR|OT, PL|URAL, Cle|aring, Hod|ges, De Kal|b, CM|ake, url|pattern), and on fixed pairs such as Highway + route number, UPDATE ... SET and 'Story highlights'.

Retrospective template-continuation head: it fires when the current token continues a repeated parallel formatted structure — a later row of an enumerated or dash-delimited list, a repeated 'Label: value' or 'Label - value' pair, a repeated '(Author et al., YEAR)' citation, or a repeated delimited code or math assignment — attending back with near-1.0 weight to the matching delimiter of an earlier chunk, with strength growing on the second and later repeats. A lone unrepeated item, a lone heading, or ordinary non-repeating prose stays near floor.

Graded number neuron: it fires strongly (0.55-1.0 of max) on a mid-sentence cardinal number, in digits or words, that a measuring frame introduces as an amount: after 'at', 'to', 'every', 'for', 'after', 'averaging', 'the first/next', or 'a/an' plus a hyphenated unit ('heated at [80]', 'every [5] minutes', 'sentenced to [twelve]', 'a [45]-minute', with the hyphen also strong). Any other mid-sentence number, a bare count ('bought 4 apples') or a label of a physical thing ('room 9', 'Version 4', 'extension 5512', 'Patient 12', 'bus 9', 'read chapter 9'), still gives weak activity of about 0.25-0.45 of max, so count it as weakly active; it is near zero for years ('in 1989', 'in 2010'), for document cross-references after 'see', 'in', 'turn to' or at sentence start ('See Figure 12', 'Table 3 lists', 'turn to page 47'), for a number right after the word 'number', and for non-number words (only 'at' after 'stored' reaches about 0.25 of max).

Dense broad previous-token head: at each measured position it attends almost entirely to the immediately preceding token (0.94-1.00 at peaks) and its strength is how far that token's value sits from the head's mean write, so it sits active-weak on most ordinary prose of 8+ tokens (peaks ~0.9-2.1, straddling the 0.25x line) and fires strongly (1.5-4.2) on the second and later pieces of a tokenizer-split word or name (Mc|Pherson, Sch|oen, Mc|Intosh, un|prosperous, ä|u, сп|и, U|.|S, there|'s), on 'is/are' directly after sentence-initial 'There', and on rare content-word pairings (fish|swam, open|wide, stops|there, The|up). It stays below the line only on (a) a one-word text of a single vocabulary token plus '.' (Water., Sorry., True., Hello., Yes.) and (b) short 3-7-token 'The'-opened clauses built only from top-common single-token nouns, light verbs and prepositions (The dog ran, The cat sat, The bird sang/flew, The man walked, The child laughed, The baby cried, The house is near the park, The dog bit the man, The cat chased the mouse); any proper name, split word, numeral, there/here/where, 'and'/comma, adjective, or uncommon pairing (swam, barked, won, wide, door, up) in the same frame pushes it over the line.

Broad head: it rests on the text's first token (strength near 0) and is active (about 0.4-0.75 x max, up to 1.0 in citation or list markup) when a coordinator or list separator (' and', ' or', ' but', a list ',', '][') comes right after a noun, name, number or adjective item that is NOT the text's first token, because from there it attends with weight near 1 to that item; the word right after such a coordinator ('the', 'a') is often active too, so predict ordinary prose of 6+ tokens that contains 'X and Y' active, and other prose mixed (prepositions after a noun such as ' near', ' with', ' into' often cross 0.25 x max; sentence-final '.' and phrase-final nouns stay near 0). Predict INACTIVE (below 0.25 x max) when the only item before the coordinator is the text's first token, because then the attended item is the resting token: bare pairs such as 'bread and butter', 'salt and pepper', 'gold, silver', 'cats and dogs.', 'Tom and Mary', and texts with no coordinator at all of 3 tokens or fewer.

Broad layer-0 head that attends mostly to the current token: predict it strong (0.6-1.0 of max) on a comma or an English article (' the', ' a', ' an') among a text's first four tokens, and predict active-weak (0.25-0.5 of max) almost every other text of six or more tokens that holds content material anywhere (concrete or technical nouns, names, numbers or arithmetic, code, lists, or any non-English language), even long plain prose, code or multilingual text with no comma or article. Predict inactive (below 0.25 of max) only two classes: (a) chains of single-token particles (up, down, in, out, on, off, over, under, back, forth, again, around, into, onto, upon, here, there, now, then) joined only by ' and', ' of', ' from' or ' by', with no ' to', comma, article, noun or number; and (b) sentences of any length that open with 'He' or 'She' and use only pronouns, auxiliaries, common verbs, adverbs and conjunctions (that, if, but, why, what), with no noun, article, comma, digit or name.

A broad head whose activity grows with how much text it has read: on the first ~8 tokens of plain prose it is silent (attention parked on the first token), but past ~40 tokens of running text of any kind it fires weakly to moderately (0.45-1.0) on scattered tokens while attending ~1.0 to one earlier content word, so any passage of three or more sentences or 40+ tokens is predicted active; even in short texts it fires (0.5-1.3) at the second member of a series - the 'and'/'or'/'nor'/'until'/'than' or comma right after a first conjunct noun ('the cats and dogs', 'between noon and midnight', 'iron, copper, zinc') - and on code, markup and JSON rows ('x = a + b; y = a - b;', '
  • One
  • Two
    • '), and it is strongest (1.2-1.8) deep in long documents on lists of names, titles, citations and code. Predicted inactive: plain prose of up to about 25 tokens (one or two simple sentences, short questions, headings) that has no comma, no 'and'/'or'/'nor'/'but', no 'than', no list, no code symbols and no repeated word; about 1 in 15 such texts crosses weakly at a stray word.

This head is NOT broad. It fires on the comma that CLOSES a mid-sentence insertion that was OPENED by a comma: an appositive, a non-restrictive relative clause, a participial or prepositional aside, or a reporting tag ('The bridge, which was built in 1932[,]', 'The plan, in my view[,]', 'designed, according to Owens[,]'). From the closing comma it attends with weight about 1.0 back to the opening comma; in standalone sentences such closers measure about 0.4-0.6 x max, and up to 1.0 x max in long documents. Predict inactive (below 0.25 x max) for: single sentences of 10 tokens or fewer with no comma or with only an intro comma ('However,', 'In 2019,', 'After lunch,', 'When it rained,'); comma-free single sentences of up to about 21 tokens; opening commas; and insertions closed by a semicolon, a period or 'and' instead of a comma. Outside the inactive class, and weak at about 0.2-0.35 x max (they can cross the line): items and 'and' in comma lists ('apples, pears and plums'); dash-closed asides ('— built in 1932 —'); a closing comma whose aside opened without a comma or with a dash. The closing comma is also weak (about 0.05-0.25 x max) when the text itself opens with a bare name or a possessive subject ('Lena,', 'John,', 'Her friend,'), but it is strong again when an earlier sentence comes first or the subject starts with 'The', 'This' or 'A'.
